qt: to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) Subject:
Lack of sufficient competition in public procurement in Greece with single bidders in 55 % of procedures

According to the Commission's official Single Market and Competitiveness Scoreboard, in 2024 in Greece, 55 % of public procurement procedures in which the relevant indicator is measured ended with a single bidder, compared to an EU average of 28 %. The extremely high percentage of procedures with only one bidder raises reasonable questions as to the degree of real competition, access of businesses to public procurement and the efficient use of public and European funds. In light of the above: 1.
How does the Commission assess the fact that the percentage of procedures with a single bidder in Greece is 55 %, almost double the EU average?
Has the Commission identified structural problems in the design or operation of Greek public procurement procedures that restrict competition, in particular in contracts cofinanced by EU funds?
What supervisory measures, recommendations or other actions does the Commission intend to take to increase competition and ensure the effective and transparent use of European funds in Greece?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.10.2026) The Commission is aware of the high share of single-bid procedures in Greece. However, this indicator gives only a partial picture of procurement performance and should be assessed alongside other quantitative and qualitative information and the wider economic and administrative context. A high share of single bids does not in itself indicate irregularity or non-compliance with EU rules. The Commission has identified multiple, interlinked factors affecting competition in Greece relating to market structure, administrative capacity and procurement practices1. The European Semester2 has pointed to challenges including the predominant use of the lowestprice award criterion, lengthy judicial proceedings in procurement disputes and limitations in the e-procurement system, which may discourage participation. In 2025, Greece received a country-specific recommendation to accelerate the judicial resolution of such disputes. The Recovery and Resilience Facility3 has also funded several measures aiming at the professionalisation of the public procurement tasks in the civil service and the partial funding of a new and more integrated and user-friendly e-procurement system. The Commission closely monitors developments in Member States, including Greece. On 9 September 2026, the Commission adopted a proposal for a new Public Procurement Act4. The reform aims to simplify and modernise the EU public procurement framework, strengthen competition and transparency, and facilitate access to public procurement, in particular for small and medium-sized enterprises. Once adopted, the new framework should help Member States achieve more competitive, transparent and effective public procurement.
